served.stem: For the gas-phase reaction A(g) ⇌ B(g) at 298 K, the equilibrium constant is K_1 = 5.0. The chemist now multiplies all stoichiometric coefficients by 2 to write 2A(g) ⇌ 2B(g) at the same temperature. What is the new equilibrium constant K_2?
served.bankWhy: Multiplying coefficients by n raises K to the n-th power: K_new = K_old^n. Here n = 2, so K_2 = (5.0)^2 = 25. Doubling K (giving 10) is the most common error.

answer.line: Coefficients become exponents in K. Double every coefficient and every exponent doubles, so K is squared: 5.0^2 = 25.

steps: Write K_1 first: K_1 = [B] / [A]. Each coefficient becomes an exponent.
Double the equation and the exponents double: K_2 = [B]^2 / [A]^2 = (K_1)^2.
Square it: 5.0^2 = 25. Same chemistry, same mixture; only the way you wrote the equation changed K.

choices.note: Twice the coefficients, twice the exponents: (5.0)^2 = 25.
1/K is the move for writing the reaction backward, B to A. This one still runs A to B, with doubled coefficients.
Halving K treats the 2 as a divisor. Coefficients become exponents, so the 2 lands as a power.
K depends on how the equation is written. The same mixture gives a new number once every exponent doubles.
5 x 2 = 10 treats the power as a factor. Doubling the exponents squares K; it does not double it.

student.lockIt: Reverse a reaction: 1/K. Multiply its coefficients by n: K^n. Add two reactions: multiply their K values.
